newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus partners face tough talks on assets.
newsitem.headline: Airbus partners face tough talks on assets.

text.p: The partners in the European Airbus aircraft consortium appeared set on Tuesday for months of tough talks as they negotiate which assets are crucial to the restructured company and their value.
Analysts and executives said Monday's statement by Airbus Industrie partners that they had signed a deal to turn Airbus into a limited liability company still left ample bargaining room.

Airbus is a consortium made up of French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (Casa) of Spain.

"There is flexibility which allows everybody to decide whether a particular asset is dedicated or not to Airbus and whether to include it in the asset transfer," said analyst Emmanuel Dubois Pelerin at ratings agency Standard & Poor's.
An executive close to Airbus said: "There is scope for lots of discussion."
The partners are likely to set up working parties to identify what assets are essential and their value before transferring them into Airbus.
The new Airbus will expand its operations to include engineering, testing, production, procurement and customer service. The current company handles only sales, marketing and product support.
A major compromise in the agreement centres on Aerospatiale agreeing to put engineering into the new company, as this transfers some of its core design competence into Airbus.
Aerospatiale's engineers are credited with designing the successful Airbus family of passenger aircraft over the past 25 years.
Aerospatiale is responsible for the valuable cockpit work. It has factories at Nantes and St Nazaire, in northern France, and the final assembly plant in Toulouse, in the southwest.
British Aerospace makes the wings for the aircraft and DASA produces some of the fuselages and assembles the smaller aircraft. Casa makes tailplane parts.
Most Airbus aircraft are assembled at Aerospatial's Toulouse plant, but putting those facilities into Airbus is seen as a fairly small sacrifice for the French company.

The Toulouse plant is highly-automated, accounts for about four percent of the worksharing system in the consortium and has relatively low value-added. All the manufacturing has been already done in the other partners' plants.
Aerospatiale, which is negotiating a merger with combat plane maker Dassault Aviation, has been loathe to lose its crown jewels to Airbus.

It appears to have extracted a major concession in freezing the shareholdings in the new company around the present stakes. Aerospatiale and Dasa currently have 38 percent of the consortium each, while British Aerospace (BAe) has 20 percent and Casa four.
The vagueness of Monday's memorandum of understanding potentially allows an "escape clause" for the partners to reach final agreement on what assets will go into Airbus.

For instance, BAe apparently considers its assets worth more than Aerospatiale's, a view disputed by Aerospatiale chairman Yves Michot, as it claims to be more profitable. As BAe cannot exceed its 20 percent Airbus share, it may ask for cash to make up the difference in value.
If Aerospatiale refuses to pay, BAe may decide to inject just the assets needed to make up the 20 percent and withhold the remaining businesses.
But Dubois Pelerin of Standard and Poor's argued that as Aerospatiale was gaining in financial strength it may pay the cash differential to ensure the Airbus company was as strong as possible.
Airbus contributed 1.075 billion francs ($200.4 million) in operating profits to Aerospatiale in 1995. ($1=5.363 French Franc)
